blocks.html:
Abstract

Why can neural networks struggle to learn optimal play in a game with a simple, efficient solution algorithm? Motivated by empirical difficulties with parity in impartial games, we use NIM to study a representational bottleneck and three ways around it. We show that a restricted model of shallow, fixed-scale quantised networks lies in AC0\AC^0AC0, a circuit class unable to compute parity on arbitrarily large inputs. This prevents optimal single-position play across all board sizes within the model. The obstruction also guides architectural design: two-frame inputs allow restoration from a known zero-nim-sum position; complementary rollout policies reveal the missing invariant; and persistent recurrence accumulates it row by row. Each route retains shallow network components while supplying additional information or processing time. Supervised experiments illustrate the benefits of two-frame restoration and multiple rollout heads; recurrence is a theoretical construction. These results establish representational possibilities, not guarantees of successful training: AC0\AC^0AC0 does not characterise practical learnability. Core mathematical results and constructions have been checked in Lean, with classical complexity results as explicit external inputs. An accompanying interactive edition connects the paper to its formal statements and proofs.

blocks.heading: sec-introduction
blocks.src: \section{Introduction}
blocks.title: Introduction

blocks.html: Game play has historically served as the “Formula 1” of artificial intelligence: a high-speed, controlled proving ground where engineering limits are tested and new paradigms are born. From Deep Blue in chess to AlphaGo in Go, games have repeatedly driven advances in search, planning, and reinforcement learning (Silver et al., 2016, 2017, 2018; Schrittwieser et al., 2020). Minsky and Papert’s analysis of perceptron limitations illustrates how representational restrictions can motivate architectural changes (Minsky and Papert, 1969). NIM poses a particularly revealing challenge: optimal moves can be found by a simple, efficient algorithm, yet learning that algorithm can be difficult. The puzzle is the gap between the ease of computing the solution once the rule is known and the difficulty of discovering it through training. Friedman’s 2017 AI challenge asked whether a system could discover perfect NIM play without being given the winning strategy (Friedman, 2017a).

blocks.html: Here we turn that difficulty into a question about computation. The class AC0\AC^0AC0 consists of polynomial-size Boolean circuits built from AND, OR and NOT gates, with a number of layers that remains fixed as the input grows. Such circuits can combine many local tests, but cannot compute global parity: whether the total number of input 1s is odd or even. This is the feature that makes the class useful here: it provides a precise model with a provable version of the parity limitation seen in the experiments. We establish the connection for an explicitly restricted neural model, rather than assuming that all neural networks lie in AC0\AC^0AC0.

blocks.html: The value of identifying a bottleneck is that it tells us what an architectural change must supply. Instead of asking a shallow network to rediscover a global invariant from every board, we can expose a useful transition, obtain complementary information from rollouts, or accumulate the invariant over time. Our contribution is this barrier-to-bypass approach: a computational obstruction guides three concrete constructions. Representability in AC0\AC^0AC0 is a necessary condition for a fixed-latency computation in our restricted model; it is neither sufficient for successful training nor a universal condition on what neural networks can learn.

blocks.html: The central observation is that while the state can be hard to process, the transition can be easy: under the promise that the preceding position has nim-sum zero, short history converts winning-move selection into local difference computation and restoration. A second route uses distinct rollout policies to extract complementary bits of the invariant. A third route processes each position sequentially, retaining recurrent state as rows and then successive positions arrive. Here a sequence of simple updates computes the global invariant, and memory connects the new position to the preceding one. These mechanisms use different resources: explicit transition information, multiple rollout channels, or a growing recurrent computation horizon. The distinction between a shallow component and the complete computation is essential. Two-frame restoration is a shallow map on a promised pair of boards. In the other two constructions, each policy step or recurrent update is shallow, but generating the information needed for a decision takes a sequence of such steps. Thus the bypasses preserve simple network components while changing the input information or total processing time. The complete sequential computation need not itself lie in AC0\AC^0AC0. Figure 1 summarises the three routes for NIM.

blocks.html: 1.1 Contributions
blocks.heading: sec-contributions
blocks.src: \subsection{Contributions}
blocks.title: Contributions

blocks.html: The results follow a single question: what must be added to a shallow learner to make the required strategy representable? We first identify the obstruction, then show how each bypass supplies a different missing resource.
blocks.heading: sec:contrib
blocks.src: The results follow a single question: what must be added to a shallow learner to make the required strategy representable? We first identify the obstruction, then show how each bypass supplies a different missing resource.

blocks.html:
• AC0\AC^0AC0 containment for fixed-scale quantised inference. We formalise a fixed-grid Boolean literal-threshold model and its bounded-unrolling recurrent extension. Both are simulable by AC0\AC^0AC0 circuits (Theorem 2.4). An attention-style extension is covered only when all its operations have an explicit implementation in the same permitted gates.

  • Single-frame impossibility for strong mastery. Under this model, no single-frame policy/value network can strongly master NIM in the worst case (Theorem 5.2).

  • Two-frame bypass via local differences and restoration. With two consecutive frames, the agent can compute Δ(P,P′)\Delta(P,P')Δ(P,P′) in AC0\AC^0AC0 (Lemma 5.4). When PPP has nim-sum zero, an AC0\AC^0AC0 move selector restores zero after the opponent’s move (Proposition 5.5). This is conditional restoration mastery, not an arbitrary-start verifier.

  • Planning analysis and the single-policy bottleneck. We analyse a restricted measurement interface inspired by rollouts, rather than a general model of MCTS. With BBB structured policies one can recover all nim-sum bits (Proposition 5.9). Root and one-heap-modification queries to one fixed member of that family expose only one unknown linear functional (Proposition 5.10). With an explicitly bounded readout, this yields the distributional bound in Theorem 5.12.

  • Persistent recurrence via sequential row updates. A constant-depth recurrent update accumulates the nim-sum over NNN heap rows and retains a summary across position separators (Proposition 5.13). With a replay of the current board or stored heap rows, this supports optimal move selection. The construction relaxes fixed total latency, not fixed-scale quantisation (Section 5.5).

  • Controlled empirical comparison and learnability discussion. On 20-heap, 4-bit NIM with 10610^6106 supervised restoration examples, a one-frame model has low restoration accuracy while a two-frame model learns restoration (Section 7.2). In a complementary single-frame experiment, multi-head FSM-controlled shootouts achieve perfect win/loss position classification while the single-head baseline remains bottlenecked by one-bit information (Section 7.3). We also discuss why AC0\AC^0AC0 is a useful abstraction for what is robustly feasible under fixed-scale quantised inference (Section 6.3).

blocks.html: 1.2 Scope and limitations
blocks.heading: sec-scope-and-limitations
blocks.src: \subsection{Scope and limitations}
blocks.title: Scope and limitations

blocks.html: Our theorems are worst-case representational statements about what can be computed under explicit architectural constraints. They are not training-complexity results, and they intentionally abstract away from several practical details.
blocks.heading: sec:scope
blocks.src: Our theorems are \emph{worst-case representational} statements about what can be computed under explicit architectural constraints. They are not training-complexity results, and they intentionally abstract away from several practical details.

blocks.html:
• Fixed-scale quantisation / fixed latency. The AC0\AC^0AC0 simulation (Theorem 2.4) assumes constant depth and a fixed-scale, bounded-range quantisation regime: weights/thresholds lie on a fixed grid whose range/resolution do not scale with the input length (cf. Remark 2.2). Architectures that rely on fan-in dependent re-normalisation, biases/thresholds growing with dimension, or depth growing with nnn fall outside this abstraction. In particular, a fixed recurrent update rule need not have fixed total latency: the third bypass deliberately allows NNN successive row updates per position.

  • Formal model vs. experimental networks. The formal units have nonnegative weights on Boolean literals and bounded thresholds. The experiments instead use ordinary floating-point signed linear layers, ReLU and LayerNorm, with Log-Softmax in the loss. They test the benefit of transition information under the reported training protocol, not the asymptotic lower bound or the deployment behaviour of quantised networks.

  • Stylised planning interface. The single-channel lower bound permits only root and one-heap-modification queries to a fixed structured policy, and requires a polynomial-size, constant-depth final readout. It is not a bound on arbitrary rollout policies, unrestricted query transformations, or an unbounded adaptive MCTS controller.

  • No guarantee of learnability. The multi-policy-head and recurrent constructions concern existence of suitable computations; we do not claim that self-play efficiently discovers the structured heads or an exact recurrent accumulator. Our experiments use controlled supervised restoration and policy imitation; self-play discovery is left for a separate study.

blocks.html: Circuit complexity and neural networks. Parity is outside AC0\AC^0AC0 (Furst et al., 1984; Håstad, 1986), while constant-depth threshold circuits (TC0\TC^0TC0) can compute it. Attention results depend on the precise model: Hao, Angluin and Frank analyse hard-attention variants, including AC0\AC^0AC0 restrictions for unique hard attention (Hao et al., 2022). Merrill and Sabharwal study the additional power of intermediate decoding over a TC0\TC^0TC0 baseline (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024); that containment does not rule out parity. Their sequential-computation perspective is relevant to our recurrent bypass, although the architectures and formal assumptions differ. Our contribution applies these distinctions to NIM policies and a restricted rollout-measurement interface.

blocks.html: Quantised inference and deployment constraints. Low-bit inference motivates studying bounded numerical resources (Jacob et al., 2018; Dettmers et al., 2022). Our constant-witness proof additionally requires nonnegative literal weights, bounded thresholds and Boolean intermediate states. These are explicit mathematical assumptions, not properties inferred merely from a quantisation format. Standard signed linear layers and scale-adaptive normalisation are outside the theorem unless separately reduced to the permitted gates.

blocks.html: Reinforcement learning in combinatorial games. While RL has mastered domains such as Go and chess, impartial games remain a useful stress test because optimality is governed by exact algebraic invariants rather than approximate pattern matching. Zhou and Riis (Zhou and Riis, 2026, 2023) studied reinforcement-learning difficulties in impartial games. Our lower bound identifies a representational obstruction in a restricted model; determining which mechanisms explain failures in ordinary neural training requires separate experiments.

Zhou and Riis \citep{zhou2022impartial,zhou2023parity} studied reinforcement-learning difficulties in impartial games. blocks.html: History and memory in RL. Using short history windows is standard in partially observable settings, where stacked frames recover hidden variables such as velocity (Mnih et al., 2015). Our point is different and perhaps surprising: even in Markovian, fully observable games—where the current state is informationally sufficient and the past is theoretically irrelevant—history can reduce computational complexity by exposing local differences that would otherwise require expensive search or unbounded-depth inference to extract from the current state alone. In our restoration setting, the previous frame carries a promise established by an earlier successful move: its nim-sum is zero. That promise makes a local difference sufficient for the next response. Establishing the promise initially remains a separate computational task.

blocks.html: Why NIM is a useful barrier example. For a disjunctive sum of independent impartial components, the Grundy value is the XOR of the component nimbers. If these nimbers can vary independently so that their aggregation contains an unbounded parity subproblem, NIM isolates the resulting aggregation obstruction. Sprague–Grundy equivalence does not provide an efficient algorithm for finding component nimbers, nor imply that every impartial game has a hard parity aggregation task. Our unconditional lower bound concerns NIM; extensions require an explicit encoding and reduction.

blocks.src: \begin{proposition}[Local restoration principle] \label{prop:restore} Suppose the \emph{opponent} moves from a position $Q$ with $\operatorname{nim}(Q)=0$ to a position $Q'$ (so it is now our turn). With multiple heads, the agent has access to linearly independent invariant measurements and can reconstruct σ(P)\sigma(P)σ(P) from their outcomes (Proposition 5.9). blocks.src: \noindent\textbf{Integration (channels vs.\ protocol).} It is helpful to reinterpret Part~(ii) of Theorem~\ref{thm:search-gap} in an ``information-channel'' language: each policy head $\pi_j$ defines a distinct rollout \emph{measurement channel} which, when iterated to termination, returns a single bit $r_j=\mathrm{RO}_{\pi_j}(P)$ that depends on the hidden $B$-bit invariant $\sigma(P)$ (cf.\ the identities in Proposition~\ref{prop:rollout-sufficiency}). With a \emph{single} head, repeated deterministic root rollouts return the \emph{same} linear functional $\ell(\sigma)$; admissible one-heap modifications give its known affine corrections (Proposition~\ref{prop:single-policy-bound}). These measurements supply no further unknown invariant bit. With \emph{multiple} heads, the agent has access to linearly independent invariant measurements and can reconstruct $\sigma(P)$ from their outcomes (Proposition~\ref{prop:rollout-sufficiency}). The finite-state shootout controller introduced above is the natural generalisation of this idea: it does not change what any head can compute, but organises the heads into an \emph{adaptive querying protocol}---the controller decides which channel to query next (and when to stop, or when to re-query for robustness) based on previously observed rollout outcomes. Then \[ \Pr[\widetilde Y=Y]=\frac{1+(1-2\varepsilon)^L}{2}. \] The formula follows by multiplying the expectations of $(-1)^{E_i}$. With fresh independent flips for each repetition, the least number of observations needed to distinguish the two possible ideal bits with worst-case error at most $1/4$ grows as $a^{-2}$, where $a=(1-2\varepsilon)^L$. Proposition 5.14 (Shallow components and complete strategies) For N≥1N\ge1N≥1 heaps of B≥1B\ge1B≥1 bits, the following constructions use polynomial-size, constant-depth Boolean components, realisable by literal-threshold networks with weights and thresholds in {0,1}\{0,1\}{0,1}.

Retaining the response board as the next predecessor gives a winning strategy from this established invariant, with the opponent to move.

blocks.src: \begin{proposition}[Shallow components and complete strategies] \label{prop:bypass-interfaces} For $N\ge1$ heaps of $B\ge1$ bits, the following constructions use polynomial-size, constant-depth Boolean components, realisable by literal-threshold networks with weights and thresholds in $\{0,1\}$. \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,label=(\roman*)] \item The two-frame selector maps a legal transition $Q\to Q'$ from $\operatorname{nim}(Q)=0$ to a legal binary-encoded response restoring zero. Retaining the response board as the next predecessor gives a winning strategy from this established invariant, with the opponent to move. \item Each structured rollout policy and the readout from the board and its $B$ outcome bits are shallow. Executing the rollouts and then the readout gives a winning strategy from any nonzero nim-sum board, using at most $BN(2^B-1)$ simulated game moves per decision. \item The recurrent state update is shallow. Iterating it over the replay protocol gives a winning strategy from any nonzero nim-sum board, with $O(B+\log N)$ memory and $2N+2$ updates per decision. \end{enumerate} Here ``winning strategy'' quantifies over every legal opponent response. Polynomial size and constant depth refer to the indicated component, with depth independent of $N$ and $B$; they do not bound the number of sequential component evaluations. \end{proposition}

blocks.html: Proof outline. Appendix C gives explicit candidate tests, first-index encoding and a fixed-scale implementation. The two-frame circuit computes the changed heap’s XOR difference, which equals the current nim-sum under the stated promise. The multi-head readout reconstructs that same invariant from the executed rollout outcomes. The recurrent controller obtains it by accumulation and uses the stored result during replay. In each case the selected move restores zero; every legal opponent move makes the nim-sum nonzero, and every move decreases the total number of stones. blocks.heading: sec-practical-takeaways
blocks.src: \subsection{Practical takeaways}
blocks.title: Practical takeaways

blocks.html:
• Single-frame is brittle to parity. In the worst case, fixed-scale quantised bounded-depth inference cannot reliably represent the nim-sum or a winning move selector (Section 5.2).

  • Three bypasses with different resources. A two-frame input exposes the transition signal Δ(P,P′)\Delta(P,P')Δ(P,P′) and supports restoration (Section 5.3.1); multiple rollout heads recover the missing nim-sum bits through depth amplification (Section 5.4); persistent recurrence accumulates the invariant over sequential row updates and retains summaries across positions (Section 5.5). The last route trades fixed total latency for a growing processing horizon.

  • Optimisation remains nontrivial. Even when a solution is expressible in AC0\AC^0AC0, discovering it from sparse win/loss rewards can be difficult; our experiments therefore isolate a dense restoration supervision signal and separately report rollout-based classification.

blocks.src: \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*] \item \textbf{Single-frame is brittle to parity.} In the worst case, fixed-scale quantised bounded-depth inference cannot reliably represent the nim-sum or a winning move selector (Section~\ref{sec:impossibility}). \item \textbf{Three bypasses with different resources.} A two-frame input exposes the transition signal $\Delta(P,P')$ and supports restoration (Section~\ref{sec:restoration}); multiple rollout heads recover the missing nim-sum bits through depth amplification (Section~\ref{sec:search-gap}); persistent recurrence accumulates the invariant over sequential row updates and retains summaries across positions (Section~\ref{sec:recurrent-bypass}). The last route trades fixed total latency for a growing processing horizon. \item \textbf{Optimisation remains nontrivial.} Even when a solution is expressible in $\AC^0$, discovering it from sparse win/loss rewards can be difficult; our experiments therefore isolate a dense restoration supervision signal and separately report rollout-based classification. \end{itemize}

blocks.html: Our focus is a restricted literal-threshold regime: fixed total depth, nonnegative weights on Boolean literals, and thresholds bounded in units of the smallest nonzero weight. In this regime, each gate has a constant-size witness and collapses to a constant-width DNF, yielding an AC0\AC^0AC0 abstraction (Theorem 2.4). Constant-depth AC0\AC^0AC0 circuits can implement approximate counting (Ajtai, 1993), yet they have exponentially small correlation with parity (Furst et al., 1984; Håstad, 1986; Smolensky, 1987; Razborov, 1987). Learning parity depends on the architecture and training setting; both difficulties and positive results have been studied (Thornton, 1996b,a; Daniely and Malach, 2020). The representational lower bound here applies only to the explicit gate model. Section 6.4 gives a complementary Fourier/spectral interpretation of this local-versus-global parity separation.

blocks.html: In this version we report two task-level notions of performance rather than full game-level Elo tournaments. Move-level restoration performance is measured by functional correctness: on a test position with nonzero nim-sum, a move is counted as correct if it produces a successor state with nim-sum zero. Positions with zero nim-sum have no winning move (Theorem 4.4); when reporting functional correctness we therefore condition on nonzero nim-sum positions. blocks.html: This experiment isolates the restoration response as a supervised learning problem. In normal-play impartial games, a restoration response is the move that returns play to a losing (PPP-)position after the opponent departs from it. In Nim, this is equivalent to selecting an optimal (winning) move from the post-opponent position: if the previous position had nim-sum 000, then after any opponent move the position is winning, and any optimal reply restores nim-sum 000.

blocks.html: The three bypasses identify different resources for handling a global invariant: multi-frame inputs expose local transition information, multiple rollout heads provide complementary channels, and persistent recurrence accumulates the invariant through sequential updates. In the recurrent route, memory connects successive positions while the growing processing horizon supplies the depth needed for parity. The common design principle is to match the information and computation available to the agent to the invariant it must maintain. We briefly discuss directions beyond the specific NIM setting.

blocks.heading: sec:othergames
blocks.src: NIM is therefore a diagnostic starting point: its efficient optimal strategy lets us separate a representational obstruction from the difficulty of discovering a strategy. The longer-term benchmark is self-play on impartial games whose strategic structure is only partly understood or whose exact analysis becomes impractical as positions grow. Three candidates illustrate different challenges:

blocks.html:
• Sprouts. Players join spots by noncrossing curves, add a spot on each new curve, and keep every spot’s degree at most three. The normal-play outcome conjecture for the standard nnn-spot opening remains open despite substantial progress with exact solvers (Čížek et al., 2026). Learning to exploit the evolving region structure, and to choose winning moves in intermediate positions, would be a stronger test than predicting opening outcomes from nnn alone.

  • Chomp. A move removes a chosen square and all squares above and to its right; taking the distinguished corner loses. Strategy stealing establishes a first-player win on every nontrivial rectangle, but does not supply the winning moves (Berlekamp et al., 2001–2004). Larger boards and their irregular intermediate positions offer a challenge beyond solved special families; the analysis of Chomp continues to pose open problems (Nowakowski, 2025). The benchmark should test move selection and generalisation across shapes, not just the known opening winner.

  • Grundy’s game. A move splits one heap into two nonempty unequal heaps. Whether its nim-value sequence is eventually periodic remains an open problem (Nowakowski, 2025). This offers a test of whether self-play discovers useful structure in component values and how they combine. Testing unseen heap sizes and sums of heaps can distinguish such progress from memorising a finite table.

blocks.html: Our results suggest several broader implications.

blocks.src: Our results suggest several broader implications.

blocks.html:
• For learning theory: representational sufficiency and learnability are separate questions. A promised predecessor state, complementary measurements, or sequential computation can each alter the resources available for an invariant-based decision.

  • For neural architecture: short history windows (or difference features) can be a principled way to bypass parity-like barriers without scaling depth/width. When history is unavailable, multiple rollout heads offer an alternative within a single-frame architecture. When growing processing time is available, persistent recurrence offers a third route, building the invariant sequentially and retaining it across positions.

  • For practice: circuit complexity can help formulate architectural hypotheses, provided the implemented model satisfies the mathematical assumptions. Tests of those hypotheses should distinguish representation, training dynamics, task distribution and computation budget.

blocks.src: \begin{proof} Multiply the inequality by $D$ to clear denominators. Write $w_j=a_j/D$ and $\theta=b/D$ with $a_j\in\{0,1,\dots,W\}$ and $b\in\{0,1,\dots,W\}$. Then \[ f(z)=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sum_{j=1}^m a_j z_j \;\ge\; b. \] If $b=0$ the function is identically $1$. Assume $b\ge 1$. Because each $a_j$ is a nonnegative integer and each active input contributes at least $1$ to the left-hand side whenever $a_j\ge 1$, any satisfying assignment contains a subset of at most $b$ active variables whose coefficients already sum to at least $b$. More formally: if $\sum_j a_j z_j \ge b$, let $S=\{j:z_j=1 \text{ and } a_j\ge 1\}$. Choose any multiset-free subset $T\subseteq S$ by greedily adding indices until the partial sum reaches $\ge b$. Since each added index increases the sum by at least $1$, this process stops after at most $b$ steps. Because $b\le W$, we get $|T|\le W=:K$. Therefore, \[ f(z)=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigvee_{\substack{T\subseteq[m]\\ |T|\le K\\ \sum_{j\in T} a_j\ge b}} \ \bigwedge_{j\in T} z_j. \] This is a depth-2 DNF: an OR of ANDs. Here depth counts AND/OR layers; counting input negations as gates adds at most one layer, as in the implementation bounds below. The number of terms is at most $\sum_{r=0}^K \binom{m}{r}=O(m^K)$, polynomial since $K$ is constant. Unbounded fan-in AND/OR gates give an $\AC^0$ circuit of depth $2$ and size $O(m^K)$. \end{proof}

blocks.html: The recurrent update. Scan mode updates the accumulator by two-bit XORs. Replay mode tests the current row against the stored summary, retains the first cancelling candidate and a fallback, and increments the row counter. Counter bit kkk changes exactly when all lower bits are one, so increment also has a shallow circuit. Mode, validity and reset flags select the appropriate register updates. Induction over well-formed token streams proves that every reachable register fits its allotted width and that the output move uses the summary from the same board’s first scan. The input protocol supplies the repeated rows; the controller does not secretly store the board.

Implement AND by De Morgan, as an OR of negated inputs followed by negation. This keeps the threshold bound fixed even when fan-in grows. Constants use no inputs and threshold 000 or 111. Thus all these circuits can use the fixed grid W=D=1W=D=1W=D=1. More precisely, for KKK output formulas of depth at most ddd, total formula size SSS, and input support below nnn, the checked compiler constructs one network of at most 2d+22d+22d+2 layers, at most (2d+1)S+K(2d+1)S+K(2d+1)S+K gates, and layer widths and fan-ins at most S+nS+nS+n. Identity buffers align layers; every output is proved equal to its source formula on the same finite input. blocks.html: The factor of two allows every Boolean level the cost of an AND gate, even though OR and NOT need only one threshold layer. The two additional stages copy inputs into the construction and arrange the output wires; identity gates retain values until they are needed. This uniform construction makes correctness and resource accounting straightforward, but is not a depth optimisation. The table proves that networks within these bounds exist, not that these depths are necessary or that training will discover their weights. A more economical implementation may use fewer layers; establishing sharper bounds would require a separate construction and proof.

blocks.html: Example 1 (Pairing strategy) Consider positions (a,a,b,b,c,c,… )(a,a,b,b,c,c,\dots)(a,a,b,b,c,c,…) consisting of pairs of equal heaps. The second player can mirror the first player’s move on the matching heap, maintaining the paired structure until termination, hence winning. The checked binary selector finds the first unequal pair and reduces its larger heap to match its partner. It has constant depth and polynomial size, and wins against every legal opponent from the paired family when playing second. For the first-player role every paired initial board is losing, so weak mastery there would be vacuous.

blocks.src: \begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:nimber-diff-ac0}] Let positions be encoded as $h$ blocks of length $B$ bits (heap sizes in binary), so total input length is $n=hB$. \textbf{Step 1: identify changed heaps.} For each heap $i$ and bit position $k\in[B]$, compute $d_{i,k} = x_{i,k}\oplus x'_{i,k}$. Then $c_i = \bigvee_{k\in[B]} d_{i,k}$ indicates whether heap $i$ changed. This is depth two after flattening the OR of the two-bit XOR DNFs, ignoring input negations in the usual convention. \textbf{Step 2: assume at most $t$ changes.} By promise, $\sum_i c_i \le t$ with $t$ constant. \textbf{Step 3: compute per-changed-heap XOR values.} For each heap $i$, define the block XOR value $y_i = x_i \oplus x'_i$ (bitwise XOR across the $B$ bits). Each output bit is XOR of two bits, hence $\AC^0$. \textbf{Step 4: XOR the at-most-$t$ nonzero blocks.} Since at most $t$ heaps changed, $\Delta = \bigoplus_{i:c_i=1} y_i$ is XOR of at most $t$ $B$-bit numbers. The locations of the changed blocks must also be selected. For each $S\subseteq[h]$ with $|S|\le t$, form an indicator that $S$ is exactly the changed set: $\bigwedge_{i\in S}c_i\wedge\bigwedge_{i\notin S}\neg c_i$. Conjoin it with the constant-size truth table for the parity of $\{y_{i,k}:i\in S\}$, and OR over all such $S$. There are $O(h^t)$ choices, each using at most $O(h)$ wires plus a constant-size parity table. This gives polynomial size and constant depth. On the single-change promise, each delta bit simplifies to $\bigvee_i y_{i,k}$. The overall circuit has constant depth and polynomial size in $n$. \end{proof}

blocks.src: \begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:rollout-sufficiency}] Fix a position $P$ with heap sizes $h_1,\dots,h_N\in\{0,\dots,2^B-1\}$ and let $\sigma=\operatorname{nim}(P)=h_1\oplus\cdots\oplus h_N$. For each $j\in\{0,\dots,B-1\}$ define the deterministic rollout policy $\pi_j$: \begin{quote} ``Subtract $2^j$ from the leftmost heap of size at least $2^j$; if none exists, subtract $1$ from the leftmost nonzero heap.'' \end{quote} Each $\pi_j$ is $\AC^0$-computable because it performs constant-depth comparisons to the threshold $2^j$ and selects the leftmost qualifying heap. Consider a rollout under $\pi_j$ from $P$. While some heap is at least $2^j$, every move subtracts exactly $2^j$ from some heap, so the number of such moves is $L_1=\sum_{i=1}^N \lfloor h_i/2^j\rfloor$. After this phase all heaps satisfy $h_i<2^j$, and $\pi_j$ falls back to subtracting $1$ until termination, for a further $L_2=\sum_{i=1}^N (h_i\bmod 2^j)$ moves. Thus the total number of moves is $L=L_1+L_2$, and (normal play) the first player wins iff $L$ is odd, i.e.\ iff $L\bmod 2=1$. For each $i$, the parity of $\lfloor h_i/2^j\rfloor$ equals the $j$th bit of $h_i$, denoted $h_i^{(j)}$, so $L_1\bmod 2=\bigoplus_i h_i^{(j)}=\sigma_j$. For $j\ge1$, $(h_i\bmod 2^j)\bmod2=h_i^{(0)}$, so $L_2\bmod2=\sigma_0$. For $j=0$, every remainder is zero and $L_2=0$. Hence $\mathrm{RO}_{\pi_0}(P)=\sigma_0$ and $\mathrm{RO}_{\pi_j}(P)=\sigma_j\oplus\sigma_0$ for $j\ge 1$. From these $B$ outcomes the agent recovers $\sigma$. When $\sigma\ne0$, let $k$ be its highest set bit. Some heap has bit $k$ set; XOR with $\sigma$ changes that bit to zero and leaves every higher bit unchanged, so a decreasing replacement exists. Choose the first such heap and set $h_i'=h_i\oplus\sigma$. The new nim-sum is $\sigma\oplus h_i\oplus h_i'=0$. Comparisons, XOR and first-index selection are $\AC^0$. When $\sigma=0$, output any legal move, or halt if every heap is zero. This selector gives a winning strategy against every legal opponent response from a nonzero starting position. After the selected move, any opponent move changes one heap by a nonzero XOR difference and therefore makes the nim-sum nonzero again. The selector can restore zero on its next turn. Every legal move strictly decreases the total number of stones, so play terminates; since a nonterminal zero-nim-sum position cannot move directly to the terminal position, the selector makes the last move. The opponent need not follow any rollout policy. Compute and retain each of the $B$ root outcomes once per decision. Each rollout has at most $\sum_i h_i\le N(2^B-1)$ moves, so their total is at most $B\sum_i h_i\le BN(2^B-1)$. This counts simulated game moves, rather than elementary bit operations or elapsed time. Multiplying by the polynomial gate work per policy update gives a bit-work bound; it is polynomial in $N$ when $B=O(\log N)$, and the displayed step bound is exponential in unrestricted binary heap width. \end{proof}
